title: As you sow
hookLine: as the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped (SN 11.10)
last: KAMMA — THE HALF-SECOND BEFORE THE ACT.

cards: Long ago, the Buddha says, a group of gentle seers lived in leaf huts by the sea. War was coming, the gods on one side and the asuras, the titans, on the other, and the seers were afraid the titans would harm them.
So they went to the titans' king, a fearsome lord named Sambara, and asked him for one thing: a promise of safety. He laughed at them. No safety for you, he said.
I give you fear instead. What the seers said back is a picture any farmer knows.

teach.b: Here's their answer, close to the Pali. You give us fear when we ask for safety. Then let fear be yours, without end.
As the seed that's sown, so is the fruit that's reaped. The one who does good reaps good; the one who does evil reaps evil. You've planted this seed, friend; you'll taste its fruit.
Then the seers vanish. And that night, the sutta says, Sambara wakes in terror three times. Two things in this strange little story are worth noticing.
First, the seers do wish him endless fear, but they don't lift a hand to bring it.

teach.h: A SEED GROWS ITS OWN KIND.
teach.b: They point to something they trust is already true: a seed grows into its own kind of plant. Plant fear, and fear is what comes up. Nobody has to deliver it.
Second, the fruit can begin sooner than you'd think. Sambara doesn't wait a lifetime.
The same night, the fear he handed out is in his own bed.
That's the farmer's view of kamma. Yesterday said the deed is the intention.
Today says the intention is a seed. Seeds don't sprout on demand; some come up in a season, some take years, and the suttas say kamma can ripen in this life or later ones.
But no farmer plants chilies and expects to pull up melons. Pali talks about kamma's phala, its fruit, and its vipāka, its ripening: the language of an orchard.

how: Buddhists often speak of good deeds as planting seeds of merit, and many make small daily offerings or acts of generosity with that image in mind.

o: luck that falls on you from nowhere
a punishment handed down by the gods
fruit: the result a deed grows into

games.q: who's who by the sea: tap the pairs.
p: asked for a promise of safety

s: the seers fight Sambara to punish him
they don't lift a hand: they speak the seed verse and vanish, and the fear comes to him that night.
in the story, the fruit begins the very same night
Sambara wakes in fear three times that night.
Pali speaks of kamma's results as fruit and ripening
phala, fruit, and vipāka, ripening: the language of an orchard.

games.q: you're one of the seers. the titan king has refused your plea and promised you fear. what do you say?
o: as the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped.
offer to fight on his side.
games.why: in SN 11.10 the seers answer that he will reap what he has sown, then vanish; that night Sambara wakes in terror three times.

practice: Picture today as a field you've been walking through, scattering seeds without looking: a sharp reply, a kind note, an hour of scrolling, a promise kept. Just notice what's been planted so far, without grading it.
Then let one good seed come to mind, a thank-you, a meal shared, five minutes of full attention, and feel its weight.

wordCard.voice: Phala, fruit. The seers' line in the Connected Discourses: as the seed that's sown, so is the fruit that's reaped.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit phala: fruit, the word for what a deed bears.

carryVoice: Your line: chilies don't grow into melons. What you plant is, sooner or later, what you'll be eating. Day three hundred seventy-three, planted.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 11.10 (Samuddaka Sutta, the seers by the ocean)
